text: You ate the last fish three days ago. You scrape something white off the wall of your tunnel and hold it up to the fire. It's soft. It smells like the forest after rain. Pip sniffs it. And he's watching you. Nine days ago, you had seven fish.
You have no food left. And nobody is coming. At least, not for 66 million years.

Forty days since the impact. Fifty since you woke up in this world. Seven fish lie on the shelf you cut into the clay. One a day. You've done the math. Seven days. Outside, the sky is the colour of wet ash. Some mornings, the ash is snow.

You remember the first weeks after the impact. A few dinosaurs made it through the fire too. One of them was a duck-bill. So thin you could count its ribs. It stood by the river every day, chewing on burnt branches. One morning, you found the last green fern in a wet hollow. You carried it to the river, broke your own rule, and walked right up to a dinosaur. Close enough to touch. You held the fern out.

It looked at you. It smelled the fern. It was too weak to lift its head to it. The next morning, it was lying in the mud. It didn't get up again. With no sun, nothing green grows. Big animals need huge amounts of food every day. For a while, the hunters ate the dead. Then the dead ran out too. It wasn't only the fire that killed the dinosaurs. It was the hunger after it.
And the same hunger is now waiting at your door.

Back home, on your mom's nightstand, there's a photo: you, five years old, on your dad's shoulders, in front of that same T. rex skeleton. Your dad helped dig it up, in North Dakota, before you were born. You haven't let yourself think about him since you got here. Tonight you do. When you were small, your dad used to put you to bed under his dinosaur posters. He dug up fossils for a living.
He'd come home with dust in his hair and a story about a bone. He died when you were seven. The posters stayed. And every night, you lay under them and wished, just once, to see a real one.
You got your wish. You saw them. And you watched the last of them die.

Back home, sixty-six million years from now, it's day fifty. On the first morning, your mom knocked to wake you for school. No answer. Your door was locked from the inside. A neighbour had to break it open. The bed was empty. The window was shut. The police still can't explain it. There's a poster on every lamp post in town. Your face. MISSING. Your mom hasn't moved a thing in your room. Your dad's dinosaur posters.
The charger, still plugged into the wall.

Your two best friends heard it at school, the morning you didn't show up. The first place they looked was the museum. When something was wrong, you always went to see the T. rex. The one your dad used to take you to. You weren't there. They still go back, every week. They stand where you filmed your video. "I'd survive. Easy." Nobody laughs anymore.

Back in the tunnel, the last fish is gone. One day with nothing. Then two. Your hands start to shake. Water isn't the problem. You still dig a pit in the sand by the river, upstream, like on day three, and the grey water seeps in clearer. Fish are. In this cold, the fish have gone deep, where your hands can't reach.

But Pip isn't starving. Before the fire, he hid seeds under the roots, the way small animals do. He's lived on those, and on bugs. His stash is mouse-sized. A handful of seeds wouldn't last you an hour. On day forty-nine, starving, you finally follow him. He walks past the dead plants and goes straight for a rotten log. He digs. And he comes out with a fat white grub. Then another. The forest is dead.
But dead things are food, for something.

So you dig next to Pip. Grubs. Beetles. And on the tunnel walls, that soft white fungus. You don't know which fungus is safe. Pip sniffs every kind. He eats the white. He won't touch the orange. It's a terrible rule. Animals can eat things that would kill a person. But you're out of rules. You eat one tiny piece of the white, and you wait a whole day. Nothing happens. Even that proves nothing.
Some deadly fungi take days to kill you. You got lucky. So the white becomes food. And the orange, you never go near.

Then you get smart. You drag wet, rotting logs right next to your door, and pile dead leaves on top. Every few days, you roll one over. There are always grubs underneath. For the first time since the impact, you have a farm. Scientists think that's how so many small animals made it: everything that needed fresh plants starved, but the things that lived on the dead kept going. Rule four: eat what eats the dead.
Every night, before you sleep, you bury the hot coals at the back of the fire under a thick layer of ash, so they last till morning.

text: With food in your stomach, you can think again. And the thought that comes back, every night, is your mom. She doesn't know where you are. She never will. You can't go back. You've known it for weeks. Tonight, you say it out loud. "I can't go back." Pip looks up at you.

So you stop waiting to wake up. What's coming is colder and longer than the impact. You'll need a plan. Your pen is dry. But the fire leaves charcoal. You pick up a black stick and write on the tunnel wall, like you wrote in the book on night one. What you lost. What you have. What you still need. Grubs and fungus keep you alive. They won't make you strong. Somewhere out there, there's meat.

text: Your dad used to say: "Every bone is a message from someone who was here."

Maybe you can't go home. But maybe a message can. Almost nothing ever becomes a fossil. One bone in many millions. But you know how the lucky ones start: buried fast, deep in mud, like the T. rex at your door. And you have a bone. The one you've been digging with since day four. It's the only shovel you have. You'll bury it anyway. So you take a sharp stone, and you start to write on it. It takes three nights.

Your fingers bleed. Your right arm still aches where the claw went in. You go over every letter again and again, deep enough to last forever. Three words. The last two are almost what you said in front of that skeleton, laughing. Except this time, they're true. MOM. I SURVIVED.

Now it has to be buried. Deep. In mud. Where the river floods. The mud at your door is frozen hard as rock. The only soft clay left is down at the crocodile's pool. The river is still running, grey and cold, with ice along the edges in the mornings. And the river has survivors of its own. A crocodile. Maybe the same one from day three. Crocodiles made it through the end of the world.

And beside it, a champsosaur: a long, thin snout, built for catching fish. It made it through too. Crocodiles are cold-blooded. In this cold, they barely move. That's how they survived: they almost stop. Almost. They're slowest at dawn, before the day warms them. So you go at first light. You crawl down the bank with the bone on your back.

At the water's edge, where the river floods every spring, you push the bone deep under the clay, as deep as your arm can reach. Something moves in the water. Pip squeaks. Once. Loud. A dark shape drifts toward you, slow as a log. You throw yourself backwards, and the crocodile's jaws close, lazily, where your hand just was.
Slow. But not slow enough to be safe. The bone is under the clay. You push the last handful over it and run.
Back in the tunnel, you sit with your back against the stone door, shaking. It's done. Whatever happens to you now, something of you will last. But you're tired of always being the one who runs.

That same week, sixty-six million years later, your mom goes to the museum for the first time since you disappeared. She stands in front of the T. rex for a long time. An old woman stops next to her. A grey braid, a sun-faded field hat, dust on her boots. "You're Daniel's wife," she says. "I dug with him for twelve years. We found this one together." She looks at the floor.

"I've seen your boy's face on every lamp post. I'm so sorry." They talk until the museum closes. At the door, the old woman says she's going back to his old dig site in North Dakota. Next week. The last time, at her age. "He always said that place had one more surprise in it."

The cold is getting worse. One night, you wake up coughing. Snow has piled against the stone door. The fire's heat melted the bottom of it, and the meltwater ran down through the gap, right onto the fire. Then the top froze over and sealed the gap shut. The fire is drowned. The smoke from the wet wood has nowhere to go. It's rolling back into the tunnel, low and grey. Smoke in a closed tunnel kills quietly.

You've known that since the first fire. You crawl to the door, punch through the ice in the gap with your bare hands, and breathe. No matches. No lighter. You try a bow drill, the way you've seen in videos, until your hands blister. The wood is too damp. Nothing. There's one chance left: the coals you buried at the back, under the ash. You dig into the grey pile with a stick. Wet. Black. Black.

Then, at the very bottom, one tiny red eye. You lay a pinch of dry fern fluff on it. You blow. Gently. Again. A thread of smoke. Then a flame. From that night on, you sleep with your head at the door, and you check the gap every time you wake.

One morning, the sand pit is frozen solid. So you work down the list on the wall. You dry grubs hard on a flat stone by the fire, the way you dried fish. They'll keep for weeks. You bring snow inside, melt it by the fire, and pour it through sand and charcoal, because this snow is full of ash. One tick. Then another. But two lines on the wall still have question marks. Your tunnel was built to survive the impact.

Not a winter. You'll need somewhere deeper. Warmer. But that's a problem for another day. The other question mark can't wait. That night, you pick up the sharp stone you carved the bone with, and a long, straight branch, and you start to make a spear. Tomorrow, you stop hiding. You learn to hunt.
A few days later, Pip doesn't come back at night. You wait. One night. Two.

On the third morning, he's at the entrance. And he's not alone. A second little face. Smaller. Pale, ash-grey fur, with a white mark on her chest. The same black eyes. She survived the dark too, in some other hole, under some other tree. Pip isn't the last of his kind.
You're happy for him. You really are. But that night, the tunnel feels bigger than it ever has. You scratch a new line on the wall. Friends: one. You stop. And you add: …and one more.

North Dakota. Your dad's old dig site. A cold, bright afternoon. The last dig of the season. The old woman from the museum kneels in the dirt and brushes the dust off the shoulder blade of a duck-billed dinosaur. She stops. There are marks on the bone. Not teeth marks. Too straight. Too deep. She brushes again. They're not scratches. They're letters.
If you could leave one message for 66 million years… what would you write on the bone? Tell me in the comments.
Stay small. Stay alive.
